column3: Before Pharaoh Aaron cast down his rod and it became a serpent, and it swallowed up the rods of the magicians (EXO 7:9-12). At the LORD's word through Moses, Aaron stretched out his rod over the waters of Egypt, then for the frogs and over the dust for the lice (EXO 7:19; 8:5-6; 8:16-17). When the princes of the tribes each brought a rod, Aaron's name was written on the rod of Levi, and on the morrow it had budded, bloomed and yielded almonds (NUM 17:2-8). The LORD had it brought back before the testimony to be kept as a token against the rebels (NUM 17:10), and Hebrews places it in the ark of the covenant (HEB 9:4), though at the dedication of Solomon's temple the ark held only the tablets (1KI 8:9). In EXO 7:15-20 the rod is held by Moses and by Aaron in turn, and at Meribah Moses took 'the rod from before the LORD' (NUM 20:8-11); the text does not say whether that was this rod.

the name or title of the king of Gerar in the days of Abraham (GEN 20-21) and of Isaac (GEN 26), and of the Philistine king of the title of PSA 34; not certainly one man
column3: The text calls the king of Gerar Abimelech when Abraham sojourns there (GEN 20:1-18) and makes a covenant with him at Beersheba (GEN 21:22-32), and again when Isaac sojourns there after Abraham's death (GEN 26:1-31). The title of Psalm 34 gives the name to the king before whom David feigned madness, whom 1 Samuel 21:10-15 calls Achish king of Gath. Read as one man, he would reach from Abraham to David, which the text nowhere asks for. The likelier reading is that Abimelech, 'my father is king', was a title of the Philistine kings as Pharaoh was of Egypt's, and Jewish tradition reads it so (Rashi). It may therefore be a title borne by more than one king, and the text does not decide whether the Abimelech of Abraham and the Abimelech of Isaac are one man or two. It is not the Abimelech son of Gideon (JDG 8:31-9:57), whose own name it was. In 1 Chronicles 18:16 the Masoretic text also reads Abimelech, for the priest the parallel 2 Samuel 8:17 calls Ahimelech son of Abiathar; that verse means him.

column3: Only one other character named Ahinoam appears in the Hebrew Bible (Saul’s wife; see 1SA 14:50). Because she is roughly a contemporary of David’s wife, it is possible that “Ahinoam of Jezreel” is Saul’s wife Ahinoam. Citing YHWH’s words (via the prophet Nathan) to David, “I gave you … your master’s wives” (2 Sam 12:8), Levenson and Halpern argue that David’s marriage to Ahinoam constituted a claim to Saul’s throne (see Absalom’s actions in 2 Sam 16:22). Perhaps David, like other kings who appropriated the harems of their predecessors or rivals, strengthened his claim to the throne in this way. - Linda Schearing (taken 4/10/2020 from https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/ahinoam-bible)

column2: the altar Jacob erected on the ground he bought before Shechem (GEN 33:20)
column3: Coming back from Padan-aram, Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem, and pitched his tent before the city (GEN 33:18). He bought the parcel of field where his tent stood from the children of Hamor for a hundred pieces of money (GEN 33:19). There he erected an altar and called it El-elohe-Israel, 'God, the God of Israel' (GEN 33:20). Luther renders the verse as Jacob calling on the name of the mighty God of Israel, without an altar name.

column2: the small gold-overlaid acacia altar before the veil on which incense was burned (EXO 30:1-10)
column3: It was a cubit long and a cubit broad, two cubits high, with horns, overlaid with pure gold, with a crown of gold, rings and staves (EXO 30:1-5; 37:25-28), and so it is also called the golden altar (EXO 39:38; 40:26; NUM 4:11). It stood before the veil that is by the ark of the testimony (EXO 30:6; 40:5, 40:26). Aaron burned sweet incense on it every morning and evening; no strange incense, burnt offering or drink offering was to be put on it, and once a year atonement was made on its horns with blood (EXO 30:7-10), as the blood of the sin offering for the priest or the congregation was put on its horns (LEV 4:7, 4:18). Solomon made an altar of gold for the temple (1KI 7:48), where Uzziah went in to burn incense on the altar of incense and was struck with leprosy (2CH 26:16-19), and Zacharias saw an angel standing on the right side of the altar of incense (LUK 1:11). Hebrews places a golden thymiaterion with the most holy place (HEB 9:4); KJV, Ohienko, Luther and Reina-Valera all render it as a censer, and whether it means this altar is an open question.

column2: the great altar the eastern tribes built by the Jordan as a witness, not for sacrifice (JOS 22:10-34)
column3: Returning to their land east of the Jordan, the children of Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh built a great altar by the Jordan (JOS 22:10). The rest of Israel gathered at Shiloh to go to war against them and sent Phinehas and ten princes to charge them with rebellion (JOS 22:11-20). They answered that it was not for burnt offering or sacrifice but a pattern of the LORD's altar, a witness between the tribes that their children too had a part in the LORD (JOS 22:23-29). Phinehas and the princes were satisfied (JOS 22:30-33). They called the altar a witness 'that the LORD is God' (JOS 22:34); the Hebrew of that verse has no separate name, and 'Ed' (witness) is supplied by the King James, the Ohienko and the Reina-Valera, while Luther has none.

column2: the altar Moses built and named after the victory over Amalek (EXO 17:15)
column3: Amalek fought with Israel at Rephidim, and Israel prevailed while Moses held up his hands on the hill (EXO 17:8-13). The LORD told Moses to write it for a memorial in a book (EXO 17:14). Moses built an altar and called its name Jehovah-nissi, 'the LORD is my banner' (EXO 17:15), with the saying that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (EXO 17:16). The Hebrew has the name as two ordinary words, the LORD and banner.

column2: the altar Gideon built at Ophrah where the angel of the LORD appeared to him (JDG 6:24)
column3: The angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon under the oak in Ophrah while he was threshing wheat (JDG 6:11-12). Fire rose from the rock and consumed Gideon's offering, and the angel departed (JDG 6:21). Gideon feared because he had seen the angel face to face, and the LORD said to him, 'Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die' (JDG 6:22-23). Gideon built an altar there and called it Jehovah-shalom, and the text says it was still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites 'unto this day' (JDG 6:24). The altar he built that night on the top of the rock after throwing down Baal's altar (JDG 6:25-28) may or may not be the same one.

the title of one anointed to an office, Hebrew mashiach and Greek Christos: given to the anointed priest, to Saul, to David, to Cyrus and to Jesus
column3: Mashiach, 'anointed', is said of one on whom oil was poured to set him apart for an office. Leviticus says it of the priest, 'the priest that is anointed' (LEV 4:3, 4:5, 4:16; 6:22). From Samuel on it is the king, 'the LORD's anointed': Saul in the mouth of David, who would not stretch forth his hand against him (1SA 24:6, 24:10; 26:9, 26:11, 26:16, 26:23; 2SA 1:14, 1:16), and David himself (2SA 19:21; 22:51; 23:1; PSA 18:50). Once it is a foreign king, Cyrus of Persia (ISA 45:1). In the Psalms and the Prophets it often stands with no name beside it (PSA 2:2; DAN 9:25-26). The Septuagint renders it Christos, and the New Testament takes that word up; John gives the Hebrew word once as Messias and translates it, 'which is, being interpreted, the Christ' (JHN 1:41). The Gospels record the question being asked of John the Baptist and of Jesus (LUK 3:15; JHN 1:20; 10:24; MAT 26:63) and answer that Jesus is the Christ (MAT 16:16; JHN 20:31); in the letters Christ stands beside his name and in place of it.

column3: Leviticus 23 opens 'these are the feasts of the LORD', proclaimed as holy convocations in their seasons, and lists the sabbath, the Passover and Unleavened Bread, the wave sheaf, the Feast of Weeks, the blowing of trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Booths with its eighth day (LEV 23:2-44). Numbers 28-29 gives the offerings for each in the same order, beginning with the daily offering, the sabbath and the new moons (NUM 28:1-29:40). Three of them, Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths, were pilgrim feasts at which every male appeared before the LORD (EXO 23:14-17; DEU 16:16). The historical books name 'the sabbaths, the new moons and the set feasts' as the rhythm of temple worship (1CH 23:31; 2CH 8:13; EZR 3:5), and the prophets both reject Israel's appointed feasts and promise their restoration (ISA 1:14; HOS 2:11; EZK 45:17).

column3: When Moses' mother could no longer hide him, she took an ark of bulrushes, daubed it with slime and pitch, put the child in it and laid it among the flags by the river's brink (EXO 2:3). His sister stood afar off to see what would be done to him (EXO 2:4). Pharaoh's daughter, coming down to wash at the river, saw the ark among the flags and sent her maid to fetch it (EXO 2:5-6). column2: the gold-overlaid chest of acacia wood made at Sinai to hold the tablets of the testimony (EXO 25:10-22)
column3: It was a chest of acacia wood two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half broad and high, overlaid with gold within and without, with a crown of gold, four rings and staves that were not to be taken out, and the mercy seat with two cherubim above it; the testimony was put inside and the LORD would speak from above the mercy seat (EXO 25:10-22; 37:1-9). Deuteronomy has Moses say he made an ark of acacia wood and put the second tablets in it (DEU 10:1-5). It went before Israel in the wilderness, the Jordan stood still when the priests bearing it stepped in, and it was carried round Jericho (NUM 10:33-36; JOS 3:14-17; 6:11-13). The Philistines took it, Dagon fell before it, and after seven months it was sent back and stayed at Kirjathjearim (1SA 4:11; 5:1-4; 6:1; 7:1-2) until David brought it into the city of David (2SA 6:1-17). Solomon's priests brought it into the most holy place of the temple, and there was nothing in it but the two tablets of stone (1KI 8:6-9); Josiah told the Levites to put it in the house Solomon built (2CH 35:3). Jeremiah says the day would come when it would not be remembered or made again (JER 3:16), and John saw the ark of his covenant in the temple of God in heaven (REV 11:19).

Solomon set them up at the porch of the temple, naming the right-hand pillar Jachin and the left-hand pillar Boaz (1KI 7:21; 2CH 3:17). Jeremiah spoke of the pillars among the things left in the house of the LORD that would be carried to Babylon (JER 27:19-22). column2: a lost writing the text cites for the sun standing still over Gibeon and for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (JOS 10:13; 2SA 1:18)
column3: When the sun stood still over Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Ajalon, the text asks, 'Is not this written in the book of Jasher?' (JOS 10:12-13); and David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, which he bade the children of Judah be taught, is written there (2SA 1:17-18). The Hebrew is סֵפֶר הַיָּשָׁר, 'the book of the upright': the King James keeps Jasher as a name, and Luther and Ohienko translate it. The text quotes it twice and says nothing else of it, and no copy of it is known. Brenton's Septuagint has no such question at JOS 10:13, and at 2SA 1:18 reads βιβλίον τοῦ εὐθοῦς, the book of the upright.

column2: the square folded breastpiece set with twelve stones for the tribes, fastened to the high priest's ephod (EXO 28:15-30)
column3: The breastplate of judgment was made of the same work and materials as the ephod (EXO 28:15), foursquare and doubled, a span long and a span wide (EXO 28:16). It was set with four rows of stones, twelve in all, each engraved with the name of one of the children of Israel (EXO 28:17-21). Chains and rings of gold bound it to the ephod with a lace of blue (EXO 28:22-28), so that Aaron bore the names of the tribes upon his heart when he went into the holy place (EXO 28:29). The Urim and the Thummim were put in it (EXO 28:30). It was made as commanded (EXO 39:8-21) and Moses put it on Aaron at his consecration (LEV 8:8).

column2: the bronze-overlaid acacia altar of burnt offering that stood before the door of the tabernacle (EXO 27:1-8)
column3: It was five cubits long and five broad, foursquare, and three cubits high, of acacia wood overlaid with bronze, with horns at its four corners, a grate of bronze network, rings and staves, and hollow with boards (EXO 27:1-8; 38:1-7). It was set before the door of the tabernacle of the tent of the congregation, with the laver between it and the tent (EXO 40:6-7, 40:29-30); on it the burnt offerings were burned, and the blood of the sin offerings was put on its horns and poured out at its bottom (LEV 4:25, 4:30). The censers of Korah's company were beaten into broad plates to cover it, as a memorial to Israel (NUM 16:38-40). In David's and Solomon's day it stood with the tabernacle at the high place at Gibeon, where Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on it (1CH 21:29; 2CH 1:5-6). Solomon then made a bronze altar twenty cubits square for the temple (2CH 4:1), which Ahaz later moved aside for an altar copied from Damascus (2KI 16:10-15).

column2: the bronze basin on a bronze base between the tent of meeting and the altar, where the priests washed (EXO 30:17-21)

Aaron and his sons were to wash their hands and their feet there whenever they went into the tent or came near the altar to minister, that they die not (EXO 30:19-21; 40:30-32). It was made of the bronze looking-glasses of the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation (EXO 38:8). It was anointed with the altar and its vessels when the tabernacle was consecrated (EXO 40:11; LEV 8:11). The text records nothing more of it; for the temple Solomon made ten bronze lavers on bases and the molten sea (1KI 7:23-39; 2CH 4:6).

column2: the great cast bronze basin on twelve oxen in Solomon's temple (1KI 7:23; 2KI 25:13)
column3: Hiram of Tyre cast for Solomon a molten sea ten cubits from brim to brim, five cubits high and thirty round, standing on twelve oxen that faced the four quarters (1KI 7:23-25; 2CH 4:2-4). It held two thousand baths by 1KI 7:26 and three thousand by 2CH 4:5, and it was for the priests to wash in (2CH 4:6). It stood on the right side of the house, eastward toward the south (1KI 7:39), and was made of the bronze David took from the cities of Hadarezer (1CH 18:8). Ahaz took it down from the bronze oxen and set it on a pavement of stones (2KI 16:17), and the Chaldeans broke it in pieces and carried its bronze to Babylon (2KI 25:13, 25:16; JER 52:17, 52:20).

Genesis does not describe them. Ezekiel saw them by the river Chebar and says, I knew that they were the cherubims (EZK 10:15, 20): every one had four faces and four wings, and the likeness of a man's hands under their wings (EZK 10:21; 1:5-11), with a wheel beside each (EZK 10:9-13); in 10:14 the first face is the face of a cherub where 1:10 has the face of an ox. Cherubim were also woven into the curtains and the veil of the tabernacle (EXO 26:1, 31), carved and set up in Solomon's temple (1KI 6:23-35) and carved on the walls of the temple of Ezekiel's vision (EZK 41:18-20); those are the work's figures of them. column3: In the fourth year of Darius men from Bethel asked the priests whether they should still weep in the fifth month, as they had done for many years (ZEC 7:1-3). The LORD's answer asked whether their fasting and mourning in the fifth and seventh months through the seventy years had been for him at all (ZEC 7:4-7). He then promised that the fast of the fourth month, of the fifth, of the seventh and of the tenth would become joy, gladness and cheerful feasts to Judah (ZEC 8:18-19). The text names only the months. They match the months in which the siege of Jerusalem began (tenth month), the city was broken into (fourth), the temple was burned (fifth) and Gedaliah was killed (seventh) (2KI 25:1-4, 8-9, 25; JER 52:4-13; 41:1-2), but Zechariah does not make that connection himself.

column2: the seven-day autumn feast from the fifteenth of the seventh month, when Israel lived in booths (LEV 23:34)
column3: From the fifteenth day of the seventh month, after the gathering of grain and wine, Israel kept a feast to the LORD for seven days, taking boughs and dwelling in booths so that their generations would know that the LORD made them dwell in booths when he brought them out of Egypt (LEV 23:33-43; DEU 16:13-15). Exodus calls it the feast of ingathering at the end of the year (EXO 23:16; 34:22), and Numbers gives its daily offerings, beginning with thirteen bullocks and falling by one each day (NUM 29:12-34). In the year of release the law was to be read to all Israel at this feast (DEU 31:10-13). Solomon's temple was dedicated at the feast of the seventh month (1KI 8:2; 2CH 7:8-10); the returned exiles kept it and, under Nehemiah, dwelt in booths as had not been done since Joshua's days (EZR 3:4; NEH 8:13-18). Zechariah foresees the nations going up yearly to keep it (ZEC 14:16-19), and Jesus taught in the temple at this feast (JHN 7:2-39).

column2: the winter feast at Jerusalem during which Jesus walked in Solomon's porch (JHN 10:22)
column3: John records that it was the feast of the dedication at Jerusalem, that it was winter, and that Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch, where the Jews asked him to say plainly whether he was the Christ (JHN 10:22-24). This is the only mention of the feast in the Bible. Its origin, the rededication of the temple after its profanation, is told in 1 Maccabees 4:36-59. The Hebrew word for dedication used of the altar, the wall and the house in the Old Testament (NUM 7:10; NEH 12:27; the title of PSA 30) never names this feast.

column2: the seven days from the fifteenth of the first month on which only unleavened bread was eaten (LEV 23:6)
column3: The law sets it on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, for seven days, with a holy convocation on the first and the seventh day (LEV 23:6-8; NUM 28:17-25). Leaven was to be put out of the houses, and whoever ate leavened bread in those days was cut off from Israel (EXO 12:15-20). It remembers the day the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt in haste, and the bread is called 'the bread of affliction' (EXO 12:17; 13:3-10; DEU 16:3). It is the first of the three feasts at which every male was to appear before the LORD (EXO 23:14-15; 34:18; DEU 16:16). It was kept under Hezekiah and Josiah and by the returned exiles (2CH 30:13, 21; 35:17; EZR 6:22), and the Gospels treat it and the Passover as one season (LUK 22:1; MRK 14:12).

column2: the harvest feast kept fifty days after the wave sheaf, called Pentecost in the New Testament (DEU 16:10)

Exodus calls it the feast of harvest, the firstfruits of the wheat harvest (EXO 23:16; 34:22), and Numbers the day of the firstfruits (NUM 28:26-31). Deuteronomy counts the seven weeks from the first putting of the sickle to the grain and bids the household, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow rejoice together (DEU 16:9-12). It is the second of the three pilgrim feasts (DEU 16:16; 2CH 8:13). In Acts the disciples were filled with the Holy Ghost when the day of Pentecost had fully come (ACT 2:1-4), and Paul planned his journeys around it (ACT 20:16; 1CO 16:8).

With it went a lamb of the first year for a burnt offering, a meal offering and a drink offering, and no bread, parched grain or fresh ears might be eaten until that day (LEV 23:12-14). The day of the sheaf is the start of the count of seven weeks to the Feast of Weeks (LEV 23:15). The text gives this day no feast name of its own; 'Firstfruits' here is a name for the rite, not the text's title for a day. Paul calls the risen Christ 'the firstfruits of them that slept' (1CO 15:20-23).

A river went out of Eden to water the garden, and from thence it was parted and became four heads: Pison, Gihon, Hiddekel and Euphrates (GEN 2:10-14). Numbers 26:30 names Iezer first among the sons of Gilead: "These are the sons of Gilead: of Iezer, the family of the Iezerites; of Helek, the family of the Helekites" (American Standard Version). Joshua 17:2 lists the same six clans of Manasseh — Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida — with Abiezer where Numbers has Iezer. In Hebrew the two names differ by their first syllable: אִיעֶזֶר, and אֲבִיעֶזֶר, whose אֲבִי is "father". The clan is known by the longer name: Gideon's father is "Joash the Abiezrite" (Judges 6:11), and when Gideon blew the trumpet "Abiezer was gathered together after him" (Judges 6:34).

1 Chronicles 7 gives the family of Manasseh another way. After the sons of Gilead it goes on: "And his sister Hammolecheth bare Ishhod, and Abiezer, and Mahlah" (1 Chronicles 7:18). There Abiezer is the son of Gilead's sister, not of Gilead.

The text does not say whether the two are one man. If they are, Iezer is Abiezer shortened, and "the sons of Gilead" in Numbers 26:30 are the clans counted under Gilead, a sister's son among them. If they are not, Iezer is Gilead's own son, and the Abiezer whom Hammolecheth bore is another man of the same family with the same name.

column3: Jephthah vowed a vow unto the LORD that whatsoever came forth of the doors of his house to meet him, when he returned in peace from the children of Ammon, should surely be the LORD's, and he would offer it up for a burnt offering (JDG 11:30-31). When he came to his house at Mizpeh, his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances; she was his only child, and beside her he had neither son nor daughter (JDG 11:34). He rent his clothes and said, Alas, my daughter! for I have opened my mouth unto the LORD, and I cannot go back (JDG 11:35). She answered, My father, if thou hast opened thy mouth unto the LORD, do to me according to that which hath proceeded out of thy mouth, and asked to be let alone two months to bewail her virginity upon the mountains with her fellows (JDG 11:36-38). At the end of two months she returned unto her father, who did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man (JDG 11:39). It became a custom in Israel that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year (JDG 11:39-40). The text does not give her name. Readers have long differed on whether the vow was kept by a burnt offering or by her living out her days unmarried in the LORD's service; the text says that he did with her according to his vow and that she knew no man.

named at 1 Chronicles 2:18 beside Azubah, Caleb's wife; who she is the verse does not settle
column3:
1 Chronicles 2:18 reads, word for word, "And Caleb son of Hezron begat Azubah a woman and Jerioth, and these are her sons: Jesher and Shobab and Ardon." Two things in it are what make the name hard, and both can be read off the Hebrew.

The first is that the sons are hers, not theirs: בָנֶיהָ carries the feminine singular suffix, and the King James prints "her sons are these" for that reason. One woman is meant, and the verse has just named two.

The second is the particle. Azubah is introduced by אֵת as the object of the verb (H853), and Jerioth by אֵת the preposition, "with" (H854) — two lexemes written with the same consonants, which BHSA and Strong's Dictionary distinguish and the pointing does not. So the clause can be read as begetting Azubah and Jerioth alike, or as begetting Azubah's sons with Jerioth, and nothing in the sentence decides between them.

What can be said is therefore this: Azubah is Caleb's wife and Jesher, Shobab and Ardon are her sons; Jerioth is a person named in the same breath whom the verse does not identify. Who else she might be, and why, is listed beside her rather than chosen between. She is held to be a woman, as every reading that takes the word to name or describe somebody does but one: read as the name of Azubah's father, it is a man's. The name itself is the plural of יְרִיעָה, a curtain of the kind the tabernacle was hung with (H3407), which is what the reading that takes it for a description rather than a name rests on.

In it every man returned to his possession and family, and, as in the seventh year, the land was not sown or reaped (LEV 25:10-12). Land was to be sold only for the years left until the jubilee, because the land is the LORD's; houses in walled cities were an exception, and Israelites sold as servants went free in that year (LEV 25:13-17, 23-31, 39-54). Daniel told him what he had seen: a great image, whose brightness was excellent and whose form was terrible, stood before him (DAN 2:31). Its head was of fine gold, its breast and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of brass, its legs of iron, and its feet part of iron and part of clay (DAN 2:32-33). A stone cut out without hands smote the image upon its feet and broke them to pieces; then the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver and the gold were broken together and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors, the wind carried them away, and the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth (DAN 2:34-35). In the interpretation Daniel told the king, Thou art this head of gold (DAN 2:37-38); after him would arise another kingdom inferior to his, then a third of brass, and a fourth strong as iron, divided as the feet were part iron and part clay (DAN 2:39-43); and in the days of those kings the God of heaven would set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, as the stone broke the image in pieces (DAN 2:44-45). John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband (REV 21:2), and was carried away in the spirit to a great and high mountain and shown that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, having the glory of God (REV 21:10-11). It had a wall great and high with twelve gates, at the gates twelve angels, and on them the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel; the wall had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb (REV 21:12-14). The angel measured the city with a golden reed: it lieth foursquare, twelve thousand furlongs, the length and the breadth and the height of it equal, and the wall an hundred and forty and four cubits (REV 21:15-17). The wall was of jasper and the city pure gold, like unto clear glass; the foundations were garnished with twelve precious stones, and the twelve gates were twelve pearls (REV 21:18-21). John saw no temple therein, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it, and the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon (REV 21:22-23); the river of water of life proceeded out of the throne, and on either side of the river was the tree of life (REV 22:1-2). column3: Pharaoh, Hebrew par'oh, is the Egyptian per-aa, 'great house', the palace and then the king who held it; the text uses it as the Egyptian court did, as the way to speak of the reigning king. The king who took Sarai (GEN 12), Joseph's king (GEN 37-50), the king of the oppression (EXO 1-2), the king of the Exodus (EXO 3-15), Solomon's father-in-law (1KI 3:1), the father of Bithiah (1CH 4:18), the king of Isaiah's oracle (ISA 19:11) and the king of Jeremiah's day (JER 25:19) are each called Pharaoh and none of them by a name; each is a man of his own, and the title is what they have in common. Twice the text gives the title and the name together: Pharaoh-nechoh (2KI 23:29) and Pharaoh-hophra (JER 44:30). Shishak and So are called king of Egypt and never Pharaoh.

At the word of the child's sister she sent for a nurse of the Hebrew women, and the child's mother nursed him for wages (EXO 2:7-9). column2: the seventh day of every week, kept holy as a day of rest from all work (EXO 20:8-11)
column3: The seventh day is first named a sabbath when the manna was not given on it and a double portion fell on the sixth day (EXO 16:22-30). The fourth commandment grounds it in the six days of creation and God's rest on the seventh (EXO 20:8-11; GEN 2:2-3), and Deuteronomy adds the memory of slavery in Egypt (DEU 5:12-15). It is a sign between the LORD and Israel, and profaning it was a capital offence (EXO 31:13-17; NUM 15:32-36); no fire was to be kindled in the dwellings on it (EXO 35:3). Its offering was two lambs besides the daily burnt offering, and the shewbread was set out afresh every sabbath (NUM 28:9-10; LEV 24:8). Nehemiah shut the gates of Jerusalem against sabbath trade (NEH 13:15-22), and in the Gospels Jesus' healing and his disciples' plucking of grain on the sabbath are disputed, with his saying that the Son of man is Lord of the sabbath (MRK 2:23-28; LUK 13:10-17).

column3: Every seventh year the land was to keep a sabbath to the LORD: fields were not sown nor vineyards pruned, and what grew of itself was food for the owner, the servants, the stranger and the beasts (EXO 23:10-11; LEV 25:1-7). The LORD promised a sixth-year harvest large enough to last until the crops of the ninth (LEV 25:20-22). Deuteronomy calls it the year of release, when a creditor released what he had lent to his neighbour, and warns against refusing a loan because the release is near (DEU 15:1-11). The law was to be read to all Israel at the Feast of Booths in that year (DEU 31:10-13). The text says that the land enjoyed the sabbaths it had been denied while it lay desolate during the exile (LEV 26:34-35, 43; 2CH 36:21), and the returned community pledged to leave the seventh year (NEH 10:31).

column3: When the evil spirit came on Saul he had a javelin in his hand and cast it at David twice (1SA 18:10-11); another time he drove it into the wall as David slipped away (1SA 19:9-10), and he cast it at his own son Jonathan (1SA 20:33). He sat under a tree in Gibeah with his spear in his hand when he heard David was found (1SA 22:6). In the wilderness of Ziph David found Saul asleep with his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster; he would not let Abishai strike with it, but took it and the cruse of water (1SA 26:7-12), asked Abner where the king's spear was (1SA 26:16), and told Saul, 'Behold the king's spear' (1SA 26:22). The Amalekite said he found Saul on mount Gilboa leaning on his spear (2SA 1:6). The Hebrew word is the same throughout, though the King James varies between 'javelin' and 'spear', and the text never says whether it was always one weapon.

column2: Jesus' coat woven in one piece, for which the soldiers cast lots (JHN 19:23)
column3: After the crucifixion the soldiers took Jesus' garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and also his coat (JHN 19:23). The coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout (JHN 19:23). They agreed not to tear it but to cast lots for whose it should be, and John says this fulfilled the scripture, 'They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots' (JHN 19:24; PSA 22:18). Only John describes it.

column3: At Sinai some men were unclean from a dead body on the day of the Passover and asked Moses why they should be kept from bringing the LORD's offering (NUM 9:6-7). The LORD answered that anyone unclean by a dead body, or on a journey far off, should keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month at evening, eating it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, leaving none till morning and breaking no bone of it (NUM 9:9-12). A clean man at home who failed to keep the Passover was to be cut off (NUM 9:13). Hezekiah's Passover was kept in the second month because the priests had not sanctified themselves and the people had not gathered in time (2CH 30:2-3, 15), though the text does not cite this law for it.

column2: the house of God rebuilt at Jerusalem after the exile and finished in the sixth year of Darius (EZR 6:15)
column3: Cyrus king of Persia decreed in his first year that the house of the LORD be built again at Jerusalem, and returned the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken (EZR 1:1-11; 6:3-5). In the second year of their coming Zerubbabel and Jeshua began the work and the builders laid the foundation, while old men who had seen the first house wept (EZR 3:8-12). Opposition stopped the work until the second year of Darius (EZR 4:24); at the word of Haggai and Zechariah it began again (EZR 5:1-2; HAG 1:14), and the house was finished on the third day of Adar in Darius' sixth year and dedicated with offerings (EZR 6:15-17). Haggai asked who had seen the house in its first glory and promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater (HAG 2:3, 2:9), and Nehemiah's covenant bound the people to its service (NEH 10:32-39). The text of the Old Testament does not describe its end.

It asked the woman whether God had said they should not eat of every tree of the garden, and told her they would not surely die, but that their eyes would be opened and they would be as gods, knowing good and evil (GEN 3:1-5). The woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat (GEN 3:13). The LORD God cursed it above all cattle and above every beast of the field: upon its belly it should go and dust it should eat all the days of its life, and he put enmity between it and the woman, and between its seed and her seed (GEN 3:14-15). Both blown together gathered the whole assembly at the door of the tabernacle, one alone the princes, and an alarm set the camps forward (NUM 10:3-7). column2: the altar of brass, twenty cubits long, twenty broad and ten high, that Solomon made for the house of the LORD (2CH 4:1)
column3: Solomon made an altar of brass twenty cubits long, twenty cubits broad and ten cubits high (2CH 4:1). At the dedication of the house it was too little to receive the burnt offerings, the meat offerings and the fat of the peace offerings, so Solomon hallowed the middle of the court for them (1KI 8:64; 2CH 7:7). Ahaz brought it from the forefront of the house, put it on the north side of the great altar Urijah the priest had built for him after the pattern of the altar at Damascus, and kept it for himself to enquire by (2KI 16:10-15). In Ezekiel's vision six men with slaughter weapons stood beside the brasen altar (EZK 9:2).

column2: the altar of cedar overlaid with gold before the oracle of Solomon's temple, on which incense was burned (1KI 6:20-22; 7:48)
column3: Solomon covered the altar of cedar and overlaid with gold the whole altar that was by the oracle (1KI 6:20, 6:22), and it is named the altar of gold among the vessels he made for the house of the LORD (1KI 7:48; 2CH 4:19). David had given refined gold by weight for the altar of incense (1CH 28:18). King Uzziah went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon it; when the priests withstood him, the leprosy rose up in his forehead from beside the incense altar (2CH 26:16-19).

column2: the two hundred large and three hundred small shields of beaten gold Solomon kept in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (1KI 10:16-17)
column3: Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold, six hundred shekels of gold to each (1KI 10:16), and three hundred shields of beaten gold, three pound of gold to each, and put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (1KI 10:17); Chronicles gives three hundred shekels for the smaller ones (2CH 9:16). In the fifth year of Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came against Jerusalem and took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made (1KI 14:25-26; 2CH 12:9). Rehoboam made shields of brass in their stead, which the guard carried when the king went into the house of the LORD (1KI 14:27-28; 2CH 12:10-11).

column2: the ten lampstands of pure gold that Solomon set before the oracle, five on the right and five on the left (1KI 7:49; 2CH 4:7)
column3: David gave Solomon gold by weight for the candlesticks of gold and their lamps, and silver for the candlesticks of silver (1CH 28:15). Solomon made ten candlesticks of gold according to their form and set them in the temple, five on the right hand and five on the left, before the oracle, with the flowers, the lamps and the tongs of gold (1KI 7:49; 2CH 4:7, 4:20-21); their lamps were to burn after the manner before the oracle (2CH 4:20). In Abijah's days the candlestick of gold with its lamps was lit every evening (2CH 13:11). The captain of the guard took the candlesticks away when the Chaldeans broke up the house of the LORD (JER 52:17-19).

column2: the ten lavers of brass, one on each of the ten bases, that Solomon set five on the right side of the house and five on the left (1KI 7:38-39; 2CH 4:6)
column3: Hiram made for Solomon ten lavers of brass, each containing forty baths and each four cubits, one laver upon every one of the ten bases (1KI 7:38, 7:43; 2CH 4:14); under each laver were undersetters molten on the base (1KI 7:30). Five bases were put on the right side of the house and five on the left (1KI 7:39). In the lavers they washed such things as they offered for the burnt offering, while the sea was for the priests to wash in (2CH 4:6).

column2: the king's house Solomon built for himself in thirteen years (1KI 7:1; 9:1)
column3: Solomon was thirteen years building his own house, after finishing the house of the LORD (1KI 7:1; 9:1, 9:10). With it he built the house of the forest of Lebanon, the porch of pillars, the porch for the throne where he judged, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter, all of costly hewn stone and cedar, round a great court (1KI 7:2-12). The levy raised by Solomon was for building it together with the temple, Millo and the wall of Jerusalem (1KI 9:15), and he made supports of almug wood for it (1KI 10:12). The text does not say what became of it: 'the king's house' burnt by Nebuzaradan (2KI 25:9) is not called Solomon's there.

column2: the ten tables Solomon set in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, on which the shewbread was set (2CH 4:8, 4:19)
column3: David gave gold by weight for the tables of shewbread, for every table, and silver for the tables of silver (1CH 28:16), and charged the Levites with the shewbread (1CH 23:29). Solomon wrote to Huram that the house he built was for the continual shewbread (2CH 2:4). Kings names the table of gold whereupon the shewbread was among the vessels Solomon made for the house of the LORD (1KI 7:48); Chronicles says he made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right side and five on the left, and names the tables whereon the shewbread was set (2CH 4:8, 4:19). In Abijah's days the shewbread was set in order upon the pure table (2CH 13:11), and the Levites of Hezekiah cleansed the shewbread table with all its vessels (2CH 29:18).

column2: the house of the LORD that Solomon built in Jerusalem and the Babylonians burnt (1KI 6:37)
column3: Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in the fourth year of his reign, in the month Zif, the four hundred and eightieth year after the exodus (1KI 6:1), on mount Moriah in Jerusalem, at the threshing floor of Ornan (2CH 3:1). It was sixty cubits long, twenty wide and thirty high, of stone made ready before it was brought, lined with cedar and overlaid with gold (1KI 6:2, 6:7, 6:15-22), and Hiram of Tyre cast its bronze work (1KI 7:13-47); it was finished in the eleventh year, in the month Bul, after seven years (1KI 6:38). At the dedication the priests brought the ark into the oracle and the cloud filled the house of the LORD (1KI 8:6-11). Later kings emptied its treasuries and repaired it (1KI 14:26; 2KI 12:4-14; 22:3-7), and Nebuzaradan burnt it in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar (2KI 25:8-9), breaking up its bronze and carrying it to Babylon (2KI 25:13-17). The old men at the founding of the Second Temple had seen this 'first house' (EZR 3:12).

column2: the veil of blue, purple, crimson and fine linen with cherubims worked on it that Solomon made for the house (2CH 3:14)
column3: Solomon made the vail of blue, and purple, and crimson, and fine linen, and wrought cherubims thereon (2CH 3:14). Only Chronicles names it; Kings tells of a partition by chains of gold before the oracle and of doors of olive tree for its entering (1KI 6:21, 6:31-32).

column2: the great throne of ivory overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions (1KI 10:18)
column3: Solomon made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with the best gold (1KI 10:18). It had six steps and a round top behind, with stays on either side of the seat and two lions standing beside the stays (1KI 10:19). Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one on each side, and the text says there was not the like made in any kingdom (1KI 10:20).
